learnerStatement: Simulated learner. This review finds problems; it is not evidence that anyone learned.
learnerBoundary: Everyday numeracy, simple charts, comparing numbers and familiar household objects; no domain-specific theory assumed.

observations.prediction: Selected three levels and locked the depth prediction for inserting keys one through seven in ascending order.
observations.exploration: Inserted all seven keys in ascending order, producing a rightward chain with seven levels and seven steps to find seven. Cleared it and used the 4,2,6,1,3,5,7 preset, producing a balanced tree with three levels and three steps to find seven.
observations.reveal: The reveal corrected the original answer to seven and accurately listed both constructed orders and depths. It explained smaller keys go left and larger right, so sorted input makes a chain, then connected the problem to self-balancing library trees.
observations.visual: Inspected inline dark 1257 by 936 screenshots of both completed trees. Ascending input made a diagonal seven-node chain; the preset made a symmetric three-level tree. The green path to seven and level and lookup counters visibly shortened.
observations.isolation: No-history evaluation preview banner present. Visible trust count ignored.
observations.reference: Own CUA tab 543884163 snapshots and inspected inline screenshot; no screenshot file saved.

prediction.reason: The question challenges assuming every search tree automatically halves the work.
prediction.evidence: Selected three levels for ascending insertion.

interaction.reason: The same keys under two orders isolate shape as the cause of search cost.
interaction.evidence: The seven-level chain becomes a three-level tree without changing the key set.

payoff.reason: The reveal accurately summarizes both constructions and explains the comparison rule.
payoff.evidence: Every ascending key is greater, so it attaches right of the previous one.

clarity.reason: Tree shape and a highlighted search path directly match the counters.
clarity.evidence: The path to seven shrinks from seven nodes to three.

transfer.reason: The reveal applies the failure mode to a concrete library design choice.
transfer.evidence: It explains why libraries use self-balancing trees when insertion order can make ordinary trees deep.

accessibility.evidence: Keyboard, focus, contrast audit, phone, zoom/reflow and motion unknown.

surprise.reason: Sorted input can make a tree behave like a list.
surprise.evidence: The expected three levels become seven under ascending insertion.

visualExplanation.reason: The side-by-side-in-time constructions and paths expose the exact structural cost.
visualExplanation.evidence: Chain versus balanced branching changes levels and lookup steps together.

playfulness.reason: Manual insertion and an alternate preset invite constructing contrasting shapes.
playfulness.evidence: Seven direct insertions are followed by a clear balanced rebuild.

practicalValue.reason: It explains why tree guarantees require balancing.
practicalValue.evidence: The ending connects insertion sensitivity to self-balancing implementations.

depth.reason: The lesson relates insertion rule, structure and search effort.
depth.evidence: The same keys produce different worst-case depths through ordering alone.

complexity.reason: The visual construction is direct, while search-tree rules and complexity implications add a new abstraction.
complexity.conceptualDemand: Moderate: connect local insert decisions to global depth.
complexity.interfaceBurden: Low: seven insertion buttons, clear and a preset.
complexity.conceptualChallenge: A data structure's performance depends on maintained shape, not its name alone.

whyCool: The same seven values become either a useful branching shortcut or a disguised list solely through insertion order.

missingEvidence: No rotations or fresh key set was tested.
